abstract: |
  We study how a scalar arithmetic Brownian motion can be represented by a
  complex exponential whose radius and angle are both stochastic without
  introducing a second Brownian driver. For
  $dX_t=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t$, $c=\alpha+i\beta$, and
  $Z_t=Z_0\exp(c(X_t-X_0))$, the radius recovers the scalar state whenever
  $\alpha\ne0$, while the unwrapped angle and log-radius lie on a
  deterministic line. We derive the induced complex Itô equation, exact
  finite-step multiplicative walk, distributions, moments, and both the
  bilinear and Hermitian complex quadratic variations. A general rank theorem
  shows that every smooth complex image of a scalar diffusion has
  instantaneous Cartesian covariance of rank at most one. This distinguishes
  the embedding from planar Brownian motion, whose local covariance has rank
  two. We also explain why the literal polar representation of a signed scalar
  process is only local before a zero and why Tanaka local time is required
  globally. Symbolic checks, exact-path identities, Monte Carlo estimates,
  shared-path strong-convergence experiments, and local-time approximations
  are preserved in an executable discovery notebook. The construction is an
  information-preserving geometric representation of one-dimensional noise,
  not a relabelling of planar Brownian motion.

# Introduction {#sec-introduction}

The symbolic rule

$$
(dW_t)^2=dt
$$

and the algebraic identity $i^2=-1$ look tantalizingly similar. They are not
the same kind of statement. The first abbreviates a quadratic-variation
limit; the second is an exact identity in the complex numbers. Nevertheless,
complex multiplication is valuable for organizing stochastic scale and
rotation. The question is how to use that geometry without changing the
underlying stochastic model.

Let

$$
dX_t=\mu\,dt+\sigma\,dW_t,\qquad X_0\in\mathbb R,
$$ {#eq-scalar-sde}

where $W$ is one standard real Brownian motion. We seek a complex process
whose radius and angle both fluctuate, which contains exactly the information
in $X$, and which is still driven by this one $W$. The central construction
is

$$
\boxed{
Z_t=Z_0\exp\!\left(c(X_t-X_0)\right),\qquad
c=\alpha+i\beta,\quad \alpha\ne0.
}
$$ {#eq-central-map}

Its polar coordinates are

$$
\log R_t=\log R_0+\alpha(X_t-X_0),\qquad
\Theta_t=\Theta_0+\beta(X_t-X_0).
$$ {#eq-polar-coordinates}

Both coordinates are stochastic if $\alpha\beta\ne0$, but they share one
Brownian direction. The resulting path lies on a logarithmic spiral and has
rank-one instantaneous covariance. That rank is the mathematical distinction
between a faithful complex embedding of scalar Brownian motion and a genuine
two-driver Brownian motion in the plane.

![Starting from a scalar state, design log-radius and unwrapped angle as functions of that state, reconstruct a complex variable, and recover the state through an invertible radius map.](figures/vector/f01_discovery_map.pdf){#fig-discovery-map fig-alt="A flow diagram maps the scalar process X into log-radius A and angle Theta, combines them as the complex exponential Z, and recovers X from an invertible radial map." width=100%}

@Fig-discovery-map summarizes the constructive strategy. The contribution is
a rigorous synthesis and visual account of standard Itô tools applied to this
specific design problem. We do **not** claim that the exponential map, the
logarithmic spiral, or the outer-product rank calculation is a new theorem.

The main results are:

1. an injective one-driver complex embedding with stochastic radius and angle;
2. two matching derivations of its complex Itô equation;
3. exact state recovery and an exact finite-step multiplicative random walk;
4. a general rank-one obstruction for smooth complex images of scalar
   diffusions;
5. explicit complex brackets, distributions, and moments; and
6. a localized and global treatment of scalar zero crossings.

# Literature and positioning {#sec-literature}

The multidimensional Itô formula and the covariance factorization
$\Sigma\Sigma^\mathsf T$ are standard. We use them componentwise for complex
maps, treating $\mathbb C$ as $\mathbb R^2$; accessible derivations appear
in Goodman’s stochastic-calculus notes and the broad survey by Pitman and Yor
[@goodman2007ito; @pitmanyor2018guide].

The distinction between stochastic exponentials and stochastic logarithms is
important near zeros. Larsson and Ruf formulate these transforms on stochastic
intervals and make explicit why continuous hitting of zero matters
[@larssonruf2019]. Brownian local time, occupation density, and Tanaka’s
formula are standard tools for the nonsmooth absolute-value map
[@mortersperes2010; @biskup2025localtime].

Planar Brownian motion supplies a necessary control, not an alternative
description of the scalar model. Its radial Bessel behavior, nonhitting of a
fixed point when started elsewhere, and winding process belong to a genuinely
two-dimensional theory [@pitmanyor2018guide; @pitmanyor1986]. The numerical
strong-convergence experiment follows the shared-Brownian-path methodology
used in expositions of Euler–Maruyama [@higham2001].

The particular synthesis developed below—designing a recoverable log-polar
embedding, stating its noise-rank obstruction, and relating it to exact complex
random-walk steps—is derived directly from these standard tools. The paper is
therefore best read as an expository computational mathematics note.

# Preliminaries and notation {#sec-preliminaries}

We identify $z=x+iy\in\mathbb C$ with $(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2$. For a complex
continuous semimartingale $Z=U+iV$, define

$$
[Z,Z]=[U,U]-[V,V]+2i[U,V]
$$ {#eq-bilinear-bracket}

and

$$
[Z,\overline Z]=[U,U]+[V,V].
$$ {#eq-hermitian-bracket}

The first is complex bilinear and can exhibit phase cancellation. The second
is Hermitian, real, and nonnegative.

The angle $\Theta$ in this paper is an *unwrapped* continuous lift, not merely
an element of $\mathbb R/(2\pi\mathbb Z)$. This distinction matters when
discussing recovery from phase.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| $X_t$ | scalar arithmetic Brownian motion |
| $W_t$ | one standard real Brownian driver |
| $\mu,\sigma$ | scalar drift and volatility, with $\sigma>0$ |
| $Z_t$ | complex embedding |
| $R_t=\lvert Z_t\rvert$ | stochastic radius |
| $\Theta_t$ | unwrapped stochastic angle |
| $A_t=\log R_t$ | log-radius |
| $c=\alpha+i\beta$ | complex embedding parameter |
| $[Y_1,Y_2]_t$ | quadratic covariation |
| $\tau_0$ | first hitting time of zero by a scalar process |
| $L_t^0(X)$ | symmetric local time of $X$ at zero |

: Core notation. {#tbl-notation}

Three levels of equality will be kept separate:

- a **pathwise identity**, such as @eq-central-map;
- an **Itô differential identity**, determined by finite variation and
  quadratic covariation; and
- a **mnemonic**, such as $(dW)^2=dt$, which must not be read as an ordinary
  finite-increment algebraic equation.

# Problem formulation {#sec-problem}

The word *representation* can mean several different things.

| Meaning | Requirement | What it preserves |
|:---|:---|:---|
| Deterministic image | $Z_t=F(X_t)$ | a chosen geometric view |
| State-injective embedding | $F$ is injective | pointwise scalar state |
| Pathwise recovery | the lifted $Z$-path determines $X$ | path information |
| Planar-model equality | the local law and covariance match a target in $\mathbb R^2$ | full planar stochastic model |

: Four meanings of representation. {#tbl-representation}

![The logarithmic spiral satisfies deterministic image, state-injective embedding, and pathwise recovery, but it cannot equal a full-rank planar Brownian model.](figures/vector/f16_representation_taxonomy.pdf){#fig-representation-taxonomy fig-alt="Four boxes progress from deterministic image to state injection, pathwise recovery, and planar model equality. An arrow marks the one-driver logarithmic spiral through the first three and states that it fails the rank-two target." width=100%}

The desired object must satisfy the first three notions while retaining one
Brownian driver. The fourth is neither required nor possible for a rank-two
target. @Fig-representation-taxonomy makes this hierarchy explicit.

Write general log-polar coordinates as

$$
A_t=a(X_t),\qquad \Theta_t=b(X_t),\qquad
Z_t=e^{A_t+i\Theta_t}.
$$ {#eq-general-log-polar}

For $C^2$ functions $a,b$, scalar Itô calculus already guarantees that the
two coordinates share one driver:

$$
\begin{aligned}
dA_t
&=\left(\mu a'(X_t)+\tfrac12\sigma^2a''(X_t)\right)dt
  +\sigma a'(X_t)dW_t,\\
d\Theta_t
&=\left(\mu b'(X_t)+\tfrac12\sigma^2b''(X_t)\right)dt
  +\sigma b'(X_t)dW_t.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-general-polar-ito}

Thus the design problem becomes deterministic: choose $a$ invertible for
state recovery and choose both derivatives nonzero for stochastic radius and
angle.

# The logarithmic-spiral construction {#sec-construction}

The simplest globally smooth choice is affine:

$$
a(x)=\log R_0+\alpha(x-X_0),\qquad
b(x)=\Theta_0+\beta(x-X_0).
$$ {#eq-affine-log-polar}

Substitution in @eq-general-log-polar gives @eq-central-map.

::: {#thm-embedding}
## Faithful one-driver embedding

Let $X$ satisfy @eq-scalar-sde, let $Z_0\ne0$, and let
$c=\alpha+i\beta$ with $\alpha\ne0$. Then the process in
@eq-central-map is nonvanishing and state-injective. Specifically,

$$
\boxed{
X_t=X_0+\frac1\alpha\log\frac{|Z_t|}{|Z_0|}.
}
$$ {#eq-inverse-radius}

Consequently, after completion in the usual way,
$\sigma(Z_s:0\le s\le t)=\sigma(X_s:0\le s\le t)$ for each $t$.
:::

The proof is immediate from
$|Z_t|=R_0e^{\alpha(X_t-X_0)}$. The formula also shows why the lifted angle
is not needed for recovery when $\alpha\ne0$.

Eliminating $X_t-X_0$ from @eq-polar-coordinates gives

$$
\boxed{
\Theta_t-\Theta_0
=\frac{\beta}{\alpha}\log\frac{R_t}{R_0}.
}
$$ {#eq-spiral-relation}

Thus the two visible polar coordinates are exactly coupled.

![The scalar path, log-radius, radius, and unwrapped angle share every reversal because they are deterministic functions of one state.](figures/vector/f02_linked_path.pdf){#fig-linked-path fig-alt="Four stacked time-series panels show X, log R over R0, R, and unwrapped angle. All features occur at the same times, illustrating the shared scalar driver." width=92%}

![A time-colored sample path lies on and repeatedly retraces one deterministic logarithmic spiral.](figures/vector/f03_complex_spiral.pdf){#fig-complex-spiral fig-alt="A gray logarithmic spiral supports colored sample points ordered by time. The process moves back and forth along the same curve rather than diffusing across planar area." width=72%}

The parameter cases are:

| Parameters | Geometry | Stochastic information |
|:---|:---|:---|
| $\alpha=0,\ \beta\ne0$ | circle | radius loses the state; lifted phase can retain it |
| $\alpha\ne0,\ \beta=0$ | ray | radius alone is injective |
| $\alpha\beta\ne0$ | logarithmic spiral | radius and angle fluctuate, rank one |
| $\alpha=\beta=0$ | one point | all state information is lost |

: Parameter classification. {#tbl-parameter-cases}

![Changing alpha and beta produces a circle, a ray, an expanding spiral, or a contracting spiral.](figures/vector/f05_parameter_gallery.pdf){#fig-parameter-gallery fig-alt="A four-panel gallery shows the geometric support for pure rotation, pure radial scaling, expanding spiral, and contracting spiral parameter choices." width=82%}

# Itô dynamics and the exact random walk {#sec-ito}

Let $F(x)=Z_0e^{c(x-X_0)}$. Since $F'=cF$ and $F''=c^2F$, scalar Itô
calculus gives

$$
\boxed{
\frac{dZ_t}{Z_t}
=\left(c\mu+\frac12c^2\sigma^2\right)dt
+c\sigma\,dW_t.
}
$$ {#eq-complex-sde}

Equivalently,

$$
dZ_t=\lambda Z_t\,dt+\nu Z_t\,dW_t,\qquad
\lambda=c\mu+\tfrac12c^2\sigma^2,\quad \nu=c\sigma.
$$ {#eq-linear-complex-sde}

The differential $dZ_t/Z_t$ in @eq-complex-sde is the stochastic logarithm
differential of $Z$ [@larssonruf2019].

There is an independent polar derivation. From @eq-polar-coordinates,

$$
dA_t=\alpha\mu\,dt+\alpha\sigma\,dW_t,\qquad
d\Theta_t=\beta\mu\,dt+\beta\sigma\,dW_t.
$$ {#eq-linear-polar-sde}

For $Z=e^{A+i\Theta}$, two-dimensional Itô calculus yields

$$
\frac{dZ}{Z}
=dA+i\,d\Theta
+\frac12\left(d[A,A]-d[\Theta,\Theta]\right)
+i\,d[A,\Theta].
$$ {#eq-polar-reconstruction}

Using

$$
d[A,A]=\alpha^2\sigma^2dt,\quad
d[\Theta,\Theta]=\beta^2\sigma^2dt,\quad
d[A,\Theta]=\alpha\beta\sigma^2dt
$$ {#eq-polar-brackets}

reduces @eq-polar-reconstruction exactly to @eq-complex-sde. The mixed
covariation is essential; omitting it loses the imaginary Itô correction.

Because @eq-central-map is pathwise, a grid increment has the exact update

$$
\boxed{
Z_{n+1}=Z_n\exp\!\left(c\,\Delta X_n\right),\qquad
\Delta X_n=\mu\,\Delta t+\sigma\,\Delta W_n.
}
$$ {#eq-exact-step}

![One scalar increment first appears as radial scaling and then as angular rotation; together they equal the exact complex factor.](figures/vector/f09_exact_multiplicative_step.pdf){#fig-exact-step fig-alt="A complex-plane vector Z n is radially scaled by exp alpha Delta X and rotated by beta Delta X to reach Z n plus 1." width=70%}

@Eq-exact-step is not Euler–Maruyama. It is exact at every grid point because
the exponential factors telescope.

The diffusion coefficient in @eq-complex-sde is $c\sigma Z_t$, a single
complex vector. It determines one instantaneous direction in
$\mathbb R^2$, even though the direction rotates with the state.

![Red arrows show the single diffusion direction tangent to the supporting spiral at several states.](figures/vector/f06_local_noise_direction.pdf){#fig-local-direction fig-alt="A logarithmic spiral has one red tangent arrow at each of several points. The arrows rotate along the curve but only one direction exists at any given point." width=70%}

The complex brackets follow immediately from the diffusion term:

$$
\boxed{
d[Z,Z]_t=c^2\sigma^2Z_t^2\,dt,\qquad
d[Z,\overline Z]_t=|c|^2\sigma^2|Z_t|^2\,dt.
}
$$ {#eq-complex-brackets}

![Discrete bilinear and Hermitian bracket sums approach their different Itô-integral targets as the grid is refined.](figures/vector/f18_complex_quadratic_variation.pdf){#fig-complex-qv fig-alt="A log-log plot shows decreasing pathwise errors for the bilinear bracket Z Z and the Hermitian bracket Z conjugate Z across seven step sizes." width=70%}

The pathwise convergence in @Fig-complex-qv is irregular, as expected for one
sample path, but both finest-grid errors are substantially below their
coarsest-grid values.

Finally, $Y_t=X_t-X_0\sim N(\mu t,\sigma^2t)$, so

$$
\mathbb E[R_t^p]
=R_0^p\exp\!\left(
p\alpha\mu t+\tfrac12p^2\alpha^2\sigma^2t
\right)
$$ {#eq-radial-moments}

and, for integers $n$,

$$
\mathbb E\!\left[\left(\frac{Z_t}{Z_0}\right)^n\right]
=\exp\!\left(
nc\mu t+\tfrac12n^2c^2\sigma^2t
\right).
$$ {#eq-complex-moments}

# Noise dimension and covariance rank {#sec-rank}

The log-polar covariance density from @eq-linear-polar-sde is

$$
K
=\sigma^2
\begin{pmatrix}
\alpha^2&\alpha\beta\\
\alpha\beta&\beta^2
\end{pmatrix}
=\sigma^2
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha\\\beta\end{pmatrix}
\begin{pmatrix}\alpha&\beta\end{pmatrix}.
$$ {#eq-polar-covariance}

Its eigenvalues are $0$ and
$\sigma^2(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$. Both coordinates fluctuate, but their local
correlation has absolute value one when $\alpha\beta\ne0$.

::: {#thm-rank}
## Rank-one theorem for scalar complex images

Let

$$
dX_t=b_t\,dt+s_t\,dW_t
$$

be a scalar Itô process and let
$F=(F_1,F_2):\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^2$ be $C^2$. Then the instantaneous
Cartesian covariance density of $F(X_t)$ is

$$
C_t=s_t^2F'(X_t)F'(X_t)^\mathsf T,
$$ {#eq-general-rank-covariance}

and therefore

$$
\operatorname{rank}C_t\le1.
$$ {#eq-rank-bound}
:::

**Proof.** Componentwise Itô calculus gives

$$
dF_j(X_t)
=\left(b_tF_j'(X_t)+\tfrac12s_t^2F_j''(X_t)\right)dt
+s_tF_j'(X_t)dW_t.
$$

The two-dimensional diffusion matrix has the single column
$s_tF'(X_t)$. Its covariance is the outer product in
@eq-general-rank-covariance, whose rank is at most one. $\square$

The same conclusion holds for any adapted two-dimensional Itô process driven
by one scalar Brownian motion:

$$
dY_t=q_t\,dt+v_t\,dW_t
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\frac{d[Y,Y]_t}{dt}=v_tv_t^\mathsf T.
$$ {#eq-stronger-rank}

Path dependence and state dependence can rotate $v_t$, but cannot create a
second simultaneous noise direction.

For comparison only, isotropic planar Brownian motion

$$
d\widetilde Z_t=\sigma(dW_t^1+i\,dW_t^2)
$$ {#eq-planar-control}

has Cartesian covariance $\sigma^2I_2$, of rank two. At a fixed nonzero
radius $r$, its log-polar covariance is
$(\sigma^2/r^2)I_2$. The numerical control below uses $r=1.30$, so its
theoretical log-polar eigenvalues are
$\sigma^2/r^2=0.4225/1.69=0.25$. This is a distinct stochastic model with two
independent Brownian drivers [@pitmanyor2018guide].

![The empirical one-driver covariance has one numerical-zero eigenvalue, while the two-driver control has two positive eigenvalues.](figures/vector/f07_covariance_eigenspectrum.pdf){#fig-eigenspectrum fig-alt="Two bar charts compare covariance eigenvalues. The one-driver chart has one zero and one positive bar. The two-driver chart has two nearly equal positive bars." width=78%}

![Normalized one-driver increments collapse to a line, while two-driver control increments occupy a two-dimensional cloud.](figures/vector/f08_covariance_geometry.pdf){#fig-covariance-geometry fig-alt="Two scatter plots show a thin line of one-driver increments and a circular cloud of two-driver increments, with the corresponding degenerate and full-rank covariance outlines." width=92%}

This distinction concerns the local covariance, not the long-time visual
support alone. A one-driver diffusion can trace a curved subset of the plane,
and a state-dependent one-driver diffusion can even have two-dimensional
support over time. At each instant, however, its continuous martingale
increment still lies in one direction.

# Scalar polar coordinates and zero crossings {#sec-zero}

A literal embedding of the signed scalar state is

$$
Z_t^{\mathrm{axis}}=X_t+i0.
$$ {#eq-real-axis}

Away from zero, $R_t=|X_t|$ and
$\Theta_t=0$ for $X_t>0$, $\Theta_t=\pi$ for $X_t<0$. Let

$$
\tau_0=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t=0\}.
$$

On $t<\tau_0$, scalar Itô calculus gives the localized identity

$$
d\log|X_t|
=\left(\frac{\mu}{X_t}-\frac{\sigma^2}{2X_t^2}\right)dt
+\frac{\sigma}{X_t}\,dW_t.
$$ {#eq-local-log}

This is exact on the stochastic interval before the zero, consistent with the
general need to stop logarithms at continuous zeros [@larssonruf2019]. It is
not a global formula through sign changes.

The correct global formula for the radius is Tanaka’s formula:

$$
\boxed{
|X_t|
=|X_0|
+\int_0^t\operatorname{sgn}(X_s)\,dX_s
+L_t^0(X).
}
$$ {#eq-tanaka}

Here $L_t^0(X)$ is symmetric local time at zero
[@mortersperes2010; @biskup2025localtime]. With constant volatility,

$$
L_t^0(X)
=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
\frac{1}{2\varepsilon}
\int_0^t\mathbf 1_{\{|X_s|<\varepsilon\}}\,d[X,X]_s
=\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}
\frac{\sigma^2}{2\varepsilon}
\int_0^t\mathbf 1_{\{|X_s|<\varepsilon\}}\,ds
$$ {#eq-occupation-density}

in the standard sense.

![A signed Brownian path crosses zero while its absolute value reflects, creating the nonsmooth point that invalidates a global ordinary logarithm.](figures/vector/f13_zero_crossing_anatomy.pdf){#fig-zero-crossings fig-alt="The top panel plots a Brownian path with marked sign changes at zero. The bottom panel plots its absolute value, showing reflection at the origin." width=88%}

![The reflected path equals the stochastic sign integral plus the accumulated discrete local-time residual.](figures/vector/f14_tanaka_decomposition.pdf){#fig-tanaka fig-alt="Four curves compare absolute Brownian motion, the stochastic sign integral, accumulated local time, and their Tanaka reconstruction. The reconstruction overlays the absolute path." width=88%}

![Shrinking occupation bands concentrate around zero, and the occupation-density bias decreases under joint grid and bandwidth refinement.](figures/vector/f15_occupation_density.pdf){#fig-occupation fig-alt="The left panel shows nested horizontal bands around zero on a Brownian path. The right panel shows decreasing absolute mean bias of an occupation-density local-time estimator." width=92%}

The logarithmic-spiral embedding avoids this singularity because
$|Z_t|=R_0e^{\alpha(X_t-X_0)}>0$ for every finite $X_t$. It should not be
confused with the literal polar coordinates of $X_t+i0$; the two
representations answer different geometric questions.

# Numerical methods {#sec-methods}

The executable supplement is
`notebooks/phase3_discovery.ipynb`. It was generated by
`notebooks/build_phase3_discovery.py` and executed from a clean kernel in the
`phase3-paper` conda environment.

The principal parameters were

$$
\mu=0.20,\quad \sigma=0.65,\quad
\alpha=0.45,\quad\beta=1.10,\quad
X_0=-0.30,\quad R_0=1.20,\quad
\Theta_0=0.40,\quad T=1.25.
$$ {#eq-numerical-parameters}

The master seed was `20260723`; independent experiments used deterministic
offsets from that seed.

The experiments were:

1. exact Gaussian simulation of a 4096-step arithmetic Brownian path;
2. pathwise comparison of the direct map, cumulative exact products, inverse
   radius, and spiral constraint;
3. 200,000 independent terminal draws for radial and complex moments;
4. 250,000 local increments for rank-one and rank-two covariance estimates;
5. 10,000 Brownian paths coupled across six Euler–Maruyama resolutions;
6. discrete bilinear and Hermitian bracket sums on seven nested grids;
7. a pathwise discrete Tanaka identity; and
8. 6,000-path local-time estimates on four grids.

For the exact discrete Tanaka check we used

$$
\ell_n
=|W_{n+1}|-|W_n|-\operatorname{sgn}(W_n)\Delta W_n.
$$ {#eq-discrete-tanaka-increment}

The sum of $\ell_n$ closes the discrete identity algebraically. The separate
occupation estimator used

$$
\widehat L_{T,\varepsilon,h}^0
=\frac1{2\varepsilon}
\sum_n\mathbf1_{\{|W_n|<\varepsilon\}}h,
\qquad \varepsilon=0.5h^{1/4}.
$$ {#eq-occupation-estimator}

The analytic derivations are the proofs. Monte Carlo estimates test the code,
scale of uncertainty, and visual consequences.

# Numerical results {#sec-results}

## Pathwise identities

The maximum errors along the 4096-step path were:

| Identity | Maximum absolute error |
|:---|---:|
| cumulative exact product versus direct $Z_t$ | $6.273\times10^{-15}$ |
| $X_t$ versus inverse-radius recovery | $1.110\times10^{-15}$ |
| logarithmic-spiral constraint | $5.274\times10^{-16}$ |

: Pathwise exactness checks; the residuals are floating-point roundoff. {#tbl-exactness}

The space-time view in @fig-space-time is intentionally three-dimensional
only to display temporal ordering. It must not be read as evidence of a
second planar noise direction.

## Covariance rank

| Model | Small eigenvalue | Large eigenvalue | Relative matrix error |
|:---|---:|---:|---:|
| one-driver log-polar embedding | $-1.39\times10^{-16}$ | 0.595978 | 0.00135 |
| two-driver log-polar control ($r=1.30$) | 0.249766 | 0.250352 | 0.00120 |

: Empirical log-polar covariance eigenspectra. The tiny negative value is roundoff from a theoretically positive-semidefinite rank-one matrix. {#tbl-covariance-results}

These values numerically expose the exact rank distinction already proved in
@thm-rank. The experiment is a check of implementation, not an independent
proof.

## Local time

For standard Brownian motion over $T=1.25$,

$$
\mathbb E[L_T^0]=\sqrt{\frac{2T}{\pi}}=0.892062.
$$

| Steps $N$ | $\varepsilon$ | Discrete mean | Occupation mean | Occupation absolute error | Identity max error |

| 128 | 0.157179 | 0.895332 | 0.832549 | 0.059513 | $2.82\times10^{-15}$ |

: Discrete Tanaka and occupation-density results over 6,000 paths. {#tbl-local-time}

The discrete identity closes to roundoff on every grid. The occupation
estimator has visible finite-bandwidth bias, which decreases but converges more
slowly. This is why exact grid hits are not used as a local-time estimator.

# Discussion {#sec-discussion}

The construction resolves the apparent tension between a stochastic radius
and a scalar Brownian driver. A random radius does not imply two-dimensional
noise. In @eq-polar-coordinates, both log-radius and angle are random because
both depend on $X_t$. They are nevertheless perfectly locally coupled, as
@eq-spiral-relation and @eq-polar-covariance show.

The embedding preserves more than a visual trace. For $\alpha\ne0$,
@eq-inverse-radius reconstructs the scalar state at every time, so the complex
and scalar processes generate the same information. Yet it preserves less
than a full planar model: no deterministic or adapted transformation driven by
one scalar Brownian motion can match a positive-definite instantaneous
two-dimensional covariance.

This distinction clarifies the roles of $i$ and quadratic variation:

- multiplication by $i$ rotates a complex vector by $90^\circ$;
- the imaginary part of $c$ converts a scalar displacement into phase;
- $i^2=-1$ is exact complex algebra;
- $[W,W]_t=t$ is a pathwise limit of squared increments; and
- the Itô drift correction in @eq-complex-sde comes from the second derivative
  and quadratic variation, not from treating $dW$ as an ordinary square
  root of $dt$.

![The notebook classifies each major statement as exact, localized, asymptotic, numerical, or heuristic.](figures/vector/f17_claim_hierarchy.pdf){#fig-claim-hierarchy fig-alt="A matrix marks the embedding, inverse, Itô SDE, rank theorem, and Tanaka identity as exact; log absolute X as localized; occupation estimation as asymptotic; Monte Carlo as numerical; and finite differential algebra as heuristic only." width=88%}

@Fig-claim-hierarchy is a compact guard against overinterpretation. In
particular, the finite-increment statement
$(\Delta W)^2=\Delta t$ is false pathwise. Only aggregated squared
increments converge to elapsed time.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

The construction has clear boundaries.

1. It is a deterministic embedding of a scalar process, not a universal model
   of planar stochastic motion.
2. When $\alpha=0$, radius no longer provides pointwise recovery. A
   continuously lifted phase can preserve the scalar path, but the wrapped
   complex state need not be injective.
3. The literal real-axis polar form is singular at zero; localization and
   Tanaka local time are structural necessities, not numerical nuisances.
4. The covariance theorem concerns instantaneous continuous-martingale rank.
   It does not assert that every one-driver process has one-dimensional
   long-time support.
5. The occupation-density estimator converges slowly because grid and
   bandwidth limits interact.
6. Monte Carlo results validate implementation and scale; they do not prove
   the analytic identities.
7. No claim of historical novelty is made for the logarithmic-spiral map or
   the rank-one outer-product argument.

# Conclusion {#sec-conclusion}

A scalar arithmetic Brownian motion has the faithful complex form

$$
Z_t=Z_0e^{(\alpha+i\beta)(X_t-X_0)},\qquad \alpha\ne0,
$$

with both stochastic radius and stochastic angle. Its induced Itô dynamics
are

$$
\frac{dZ_t}{Z_t}
=\left[
(\alpha+i\beta)\mu
+\frac12(\alpha+i\beta)^2\sigma^2
\right]dt
+(\alpha+i\beta)\sigma\,dW_t,
$$

and its exact random-walk step is

$$
Z_{n+1}
=Z_n\exp\!\left[
(\alpha+i\beta)
(\mu\Delta t+\sigma\Delta W_n)
\right].
$$

The radius reconstructs $X_t$; the angle supplies a geometric rotation; and
the shared Brownian increment forces rank-one local covariance. A genuine
planar Brownian motion remains a different, rank-two, two-driver model. At
scalar zero crossings, the ordinary polar logarithm must give way to
localization and Tanaka local time.

The bridge between complex numbers and Itô calculus is therefore precise but
limited: complex exponentials organize stochastic scale and rotation, while
quadratic variation—not the algebraic identity $i^2=-1$—produces the Itô
correction.

# Appendix A. Expanded Itô algebra {#sec-appendix-ito}

Starting from @eq-polar-reconstruction and @eq-linear-polar-sde,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\frac{dZ}{Z}
&=\alpha\mu\,dt+\alpha\sigma\,dW
  +i\beta\mu\,dt+i\beta\sigma\,dW\\
&\quad+\frac12(\alpha^2-\beta^2)\sigma^2dt
  +i\alpha\beta\sigma^2dt\\
&=\left[
(\alpha+i\beta)\mu
+\frac12(\alpha^2-\beta^2+2i\alpha\beta)\sigma^2
\right]dt\\
&\quad+(\alpha+i\beta)\sigma\,dW\\
&=\left(c\mu+\frac12c^2\sigma^2\right)dt+c\sigma\,dW.
\end{aligned}
$$

The symbolic notebook independently simplifies the difference between the
direct and polar drifts to zero.

# Appendix B. Exact moment derivation {#sec-appendix-moments}

For any complex $q$, the entire Gaussian moment-generating function gives

$$
\mathbb E[e^{qY_t}]
=\exp\!\left(q\mu t+\tfrac12q^2\sigma^2t\right),
\qquad Y_t=X_t-X_0.
$$

Taking $q=p\alpha$ and multiplying by $R_0^p$ gives
@eq-radial-moments. Taking $q=nc$ gives @eq-complex-moments. No complex
branch choice appears because the random variable is defined by the entire
exponential function, not by applying a logarithm to sampled $Z_t$.

```bash
conda run -n phase3-paper python \
  paper/notebooks/build_phase3_discovery.py

conda run -n phase3-paper jupyter nbconvert \
  --to notebook --execute --inplace \
  --ExecutePreprocessor.timeout=900 \
  paper/notebooks/phase3_discovery.ipynb
```

```bash
quarto render paper --to pdf
```

The notebook writes all figure sources to `paper/figures/`, all numerical
tables to `paper/tables/`, and a machine-readable summary to
`paper/tables/numerical_summary.json`.
